title: Asking politely
job: Requests, thanks, apologies in the right register
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The imperative is the ta- form with its prefix taken off: tashrab → ishrab, tadhhab → idhhab, ta'kul → kul. If what is left cannot start a word, a vowel goes in front, and word-initial hamza is not written — so these are spelled with a plain vowel.

Arabic has no polite verb form above the imperative. Politeness is bought with words — min faḍlika, law samaḥta — or by asking instead of telling. Looking for a politer conjugation is the English and Hindi habit, and there is nothing there to find.
The second person forks by GENDER, not by politeness: -ka to a man, -ki to a woman. Arabic has no tú/usted split at all, and the course has been marking this since its first module.
hal yumkinuka an + verb is "is it possible for you to…", built from hal (M2) and an (M3), both already yours. It is the softest of the three ways to ask.
The adverbial -an ending survives the course's no-case-endings rule, because it is lexical rather than grammatical: shukran, jazīlan, ʿafwan, ghadan, dāʾiman.

The romanized line and the Arabic line do not carry the same information. samaḥta and samaḥti are one spelling in unvowelled Arabic — سمحت — and two in the romanization. The line you read tells you who is being addressed; the quiet line does not.

words.note: tashrab (M4) with the prefix taken off, and an i- put in front because shr- cannot start a word. To a woman it adds -ī: ishrabī.

sentences.trap: An imperative on its own is not rude in Arabic, but it is bare. min faḍlika is what a speaker adds, and it is added almost every time.
sentences.sound: ISH-rab, with the initial i barely there — in fast speech it disappears after a vowel.

sentences.usage: Offered rather than ordered: this is what a host says while pouring. min faḍlika turns it from an instruction into an invitation.
sentences.mnemonic: Take the prefix off and put a vowel where it stood.

words.note: Only ever appears in this phrase in the course. law samaḥta is frozen — literally "if you would permit" — and neither word is used apart from it here.
The perfect's person-suffix, which the course writes in full: -ta to a man, -ti to a woman. Both are سمحت in the Arabic line — the quiet line cannot tell them apart.

sentences.trap: The two forms are one spelling in Arabic and two in the romanization. This is the first place in the course where the two lines carry different amounts of information.
sentences.sound: law sa-MAḤ-ta. The ḥ is a hard breath from deep in the throat, not an English h.

sentences.usage: The everyday way to stop a stranger, anywhere Arabic is spoken. Chipped formal because it is the ceremonial end of the course's one register.
sentences.mnemonic: The romanization knows who you are talking to; the script leaves it to the room.

words.cue: is it possible for you (to a man)
words.note: Literally "it is possible for you", with the same -ka / -ki suffix as ismuka. The two are one spelling in the Arabic line, as samaḥta and samaḥti are.

sentences.trap: The frame has no word for "can" and no word for "could". Arabic asks whether something is possible FOR you, and the softness comes from the length of the question.
sentences.sound: yum-KI-nu-ka, four syllables, and every one of them said.

variations.cue: Could you drink the coffee? (to a woman)
variations.changed: the frame moves to the feminine — and the Arabic line does not
a different verb after an
a request for a favour rather than for a moment

mistake.why: an is obligatory between the two verbs, exactly as it is after urīd (M3). Two verbs never touch.

sentences.usage: The softest request in the module, and the one that is safe with anybody at all.
sentences.mnemonic: Not can you, but is it possible for you.

words.note: An imperative with -nī, "me", glued to the end. Word-initial hamza is not written, so it starts with a plain a — and the ʿ in the middle is ʿayn, a different letter.

sentences.trap: The object pronoun attaches to the verb as one word. Arabic has nothing loose for a learner to place, and nothing to place wrongly.
sentences.sound: aʿ-ṬI-nī. The ʿ is ʿayn — a tightening at the very bottom of the throat, not the hamza's clean catch.

the other softener, and a bare noun

mistake.why: The pronoun is part of the word: aʿṭinī. Arabic never lets an object pronoun stand alone after a verb.

sentences.usage: A counter, a table, a shop. Direct, and completely ordinary once min faḍlika is on the end.
sentences.mnemonic: The me is glued on, not set down beside it.

sentences.cue: Thank you very much for the juice

words.note: Only ever follows shukran, and it carries the same adverbial -an. The pair is a fixed step above M2's bare shukran.

sentences.trap: ʿalā is "on" or "upon" and here it is "for". Thanks in Arabic land ON the thing given, not for it.
sentences.sound: SHUK-ran ja-ZĪ-lan — both -an endings are a light n, and neither is a case ending.

mistake.why: The -an is part of the phrase: jazīlan. It is one of the three exemptions from the course's no-case-endings rule.

sentences.usage: One step above shukran and well short of ceremony. It is what you say when someone has actually done something.
sentences.mnemonic: Thanks fall ON the thing, and they come in an -an.

words.note: Only appears after lā, and the pair means "no harm done" or "never mind". The hamza in the middle is written ʾ and is a different letter from ʿayn.

sentences.trap: ʿafwan answers thanks AND excuses an interruption. One word, two jobs, and its row is M10's from the level below.
sentences.sound: ʿAF-wan, and BAʾ-sa with a clean catch in the throat between the a and the s.

mistake.why: The phrase is lā baʾsa, with the final -a. It is frozen, and dropping the vowel leaves half a phrase.

sentences.usage: The reply to thanks, and the reply to an apology. It closes a small exchange without ending the conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: No harm, so nothing to answer for.

sentences.cue: Sorry, I don't want the coffee

words.note: An adjective, so it agrees with the SPEAKER: āsif from a man, āsifa from a woman. It is regret, not the word for stopping a stranger.

sentences.trap: āsif agrees with whoever is speaking, which is the opposite of the L1 rule that adjectives agree with what they describe — because here the speaker IS what is described.
sentences.sound: Ā-sif, with a long first vowel. The Arabic line writes it with a madda, آ, which is two hamzas' worth of a.

mistake.why: A woman says āsifa. The adjective follows the speaker, because the speaker is the one who is sorry.

sentences.usage: Turning something down. Adding a reason after it is what keeps it warm, and in Arabic hosting the offer will come again anyway.
sentences.mnemonic: The sorry one is the one it agrees with.

words.note: From taʾkul with the prefix off, and the hamza falls away with it — kul, not ʾkul. Three letters, and it is the whole imperative.

sentences.trap: No vowel goes in front here, because kul can already start a word. The rule adds one only when it has to.
sentences.sound: KUL, one syllable, with the l clear and forward.
